Oracle Database

Source: vignettes/oracle.Rmd
oracle.Rmd

Use oauth_db_oracle() to query Oracle Database with each visitor’s OAuth access token. It returns a DBI connection for SQL and dbplyr. Oracle must trust the token’s provider and map the visitor to database privileges.

The helper supports two authorization models:

Model Oracle setup Helper argument
Global schema A database global user mapped to an external identity; existing Entra configurations use this model authorization_model = "global" (default)
End-user context Oracle Deep Data Security direct logon with user data roles, including configured OCI IAM OAuth and Keycloak integrations authorization_model = "end_user"

For OAuth-protected HTTP resources, use the separate Oracle REST Data Services guide.

Set up the database and driver

Ask your administrator for a TCPS listener address, port, service name, trusted identity provider and database access scope. The server needs the corresponding global-schema or data-role mappings. Signing in to the Shiny app does not create those mappings.

Choose the provider setup that matches your deployment:

  • Microsoft Entra: configure the Entra database integration. Existing global-schema configurations use "global"; Deep Data Security direct-logon configurations use "end_user".
  • OCI IAM Identity Domains OAuth: configure IDENTITY_PROVIDER_TYPE=OCI_IAM and the database’s OAuth application and domain. Oracle documents the OAuth configuration parameter from Oracle 26ai RU 23.26.2. Follow the database’s supported administrative setup, particularly for Autonomous Database. This is an OAuth bearer-token flow, separate from OCI IAM proof-of-possession authentication.
  • Keycloak: Oracle’s current 26ai Deep Data Security guide documents IDENTITY_PROVIDER_TYPE=OAUTH2 with issuer, JWKS, audience and claim mappings. Keycloak is the initial supported configurable provider; this integration is unavailable on Autonomous Database. Follow database IAM configuration and the direct-login procedure.

Install the R package odbc and Oracle Instant Client’s Basic and ODBC packages for the architecture of your R process. Register the Oracle ODBC driver and find its name with odbc::odbcListDrivers(). Use a current supported Oracle client with the required token integration. The Entra thick-client path is documented from 19c 19.16, excluding the 21c thick client. OCI IAM OAuth and configurable-provider Deep Data Security require newer database features and a compatible current client. Check your actual server release, update level and driver against Oracle’s ODBC setup guide and client support table.

The client needs a trusted TLS certificate chain. Depending on the client, platform and database, use its configured trust store or pass an Oracle wallet directory as wallet_location. A database requiring mutual TLS also needs the client certificate in that wallet. Use server_cert_dn when your administrator supplies the expected certificate distinguished name; otherwise the client matches the hostname. Certificate matching is always enabled.

For OCI IAM OAuth, Oracle’s direct-login procedure specifies the server certificate DN. Copy it from the administrator’s connection details (or the downloaded Autonomous wallet alias) into server_cert_dn when calling the helper. Use the matching wallet when the service requires mutual TLS.

Register the Shiny application

Register an authorization-code client with PKCE at the provider trusted by the database. Register http://localhost:8100 as its redirect URI. The app needs the database access scope and the corresponding user or group assignments. Configure the provider to issue the database audience and required identity and role claims. For Keycloak, configure an audience mapper and a top-level role claim matching Oracle’s provider configuration.

The complete app below uses OIDC discovery for a Keycloak or OCI IAM Identity Domains provider with OpenID Connect enabled. Its "end_user" mode requires Oracle Deep Data Security direct logon. Enable refresh-token issuance when requesting offline_access, or replace that scope with your provider’s documented refresh setup. An Entra alternative follows the app.

Save the app settings in your local .Renviron and restart R:

OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID=your-shiny-app-client-id
OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET=your-shiny-app-client-secret
OAUTHDB_ORACLE_ISSUER=https://login.example.org/realms/reporting
OAUTHDB_ORACLE_SCOPE=database.read
OAUTHDB_ORACLE_HOST=database.example.org
OAUTHDB_ORACLE_SERVICE=reporting.example.org
OAUTHDB_ORACLE_DRIVER=Oracle in instantclient_19_30
Setting Where to find it
OAUTHDB_ORACLE_ISSUER OIDC issuer configured for the database’s provider
OAUTHDB_ORACLE_SCOPE Exact database access scope supplied by the administrator; OCI IAM uses the resource audience concatenated with the scope name
Host, service and TCPS port Oracle connection details supplied by the administrator
Driver Installed driver name reported by odbc::odbcListDrivers()
Wallet and certificate DN, if needed Oracle administrator’s TLS configuration

A complete app

The scope name below is checked literally. Configure the token audience on the authorization server for this client and database:

library(shiny)
library(shinyOAuth)
library(shinyOAuthDB)

scope <- Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_ORACLE_SCOPE")
provider <- oauth_provider_oidc_discover(
  issuer = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_ORACLE_ISSUER")
)
client <- oauth_client(
  provider,
  client_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID"),
  client_secret = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET"),
  redirect_uri = "http://localhost:8100",
  scopes = c("openid", "profile", "offline_access", scope),
  required_scopes = scope
)

ui <- oauth_ui(
  fluidPage(
    actionButton("login", "Sign in"),
    actionButton("logout", "Sign out"),
    tableOutput("rows")
  ),
  id = "auth",
  client = client
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  auth <- oauth_module_server("auth", client, auto_redirect = FALSE)
  observeEvent(input$login, auth$request_login())
  observeEvent(input$logout, auth$logout())

  con <- oauth_db_oracle(
    auth$connection,
    host = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_ORACLE_HOST"),
    service_name = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_ORACLE_SERVICE"),
    driver = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_ORACLE_DRIVER"),
    port = 1522L,
    authorization_model = "end_user"
  )
  output$rows <- renderTable({
    connection <- con()
    DBI::dbGetQuery(
      connection,
      "SELECT ORA_END_USER_CONTEXT.username AS database_user FROM DUAL"
    )
  })
}

runApp(
  shinyApp(ui, server, uiPattern = ".*"),
  port = 8100,
  launch.browser = FALSE
)

Save the code as example.R, set your TCPS port and any wallet or certificate DN arguments, then run source("example.R"). Open http://localhost:8100 in your regular browser and sign in. The example shows the Oracle end-user identity. Replace the query with a table or view the user can read.

Microsoft Entra alternative

For Entra, use the Microsoft client with a custom database resource target. Register a Web application with the same redirect URI and the database’s delegated permission, commonly session:scope:connect. Your administrator must configure global-schema or data-role mappings and access-token claims; Entra v2 setup includes the upn claim. See Oracle’s registration example and Microsoft app registration.

resource <- Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_ORACLE_RESOURCE")
scope <- paste0(resource, "/session:scope:connect")
client <- oauth_db_microsoft_client(
  tenant_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_TENANT_ID"),
  client_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID"),
  client_secret = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET"),
  redirect_uri = "http://localhost:8100",
  token_targets = list(
    oracle = list(resource = resource, scopes = scope, required_scopes = scope)
  )
)

OAUTHDB_ORACLE_RESOURCE is the database server’s Entra Application ID URI, not the Shiny application’s client ID. In the app’s connection helper, set target = "oracle". For an existing global-schema deployment, set authorization_model = "global" and query SELECT USER FROM DUAL to inspect the database schema identity. For Deep Data Security use authorization_model = "end_user" and retain the end-user identity query. Keep /.default consent markers in client settings; required_scopes now treats every provider’s scope names literally.

Connections and token files

shinyOAuth handles browser sign-in and token renewal. The adapter obtains the current access token when opening a connection. It supplies a separate Oracle Net descriptor containing TOKEN_AUTH=OAUTH and the location of a temporary token file. It does not change shared Oracle configuration files or the process’s TNS_ADMIN environment variable.

The token file is removed after connection opening, including on error or interrupt. On Unix, its directory is private (0700) and the file has mode 0600. On Windows, use a private R temporary directory because access rules are inherited from its parent directory.

Before returning a connection, the helper verifies the chosen model:

  • "global" requires SYS_CONTEXT('USERENV', 'AUTHENTICATION_METHOD') to report TOKEN_GLOBAL.
  • "end_user" reads only issuer, subject and audience from Oracle’s system-managed ORA_END_USER_CONTEXT.USER.TOKEN and requires them to match the submitted JWT. Local decoding establishes the expected claims; Oracle validates the token and establishes the context. Missing or mismatched context closes the connection, even if a global-schema login succeeded. This prevents global-user precedence from silently bypassing the requested Deep Data Security model.

Global-schema connections survive ordinary token renewal. End-user connections reopen on the next con() call when the token changes, so updated role claims reach the database. This does not replay completed reactive queries. Account changes, permission loss, sign-out and Shiny session end close both types. Always call con() before each operation.

The helper disables Oracle ODBC failover. Reopen a broken connection by calling con() so the new connection gets a current token. It does not implement OCI IAM proof-of-possession authentication, password login, proxy-user connections or application-mediated two-token contexts.

Automated checks cover ODBC arguments, token and context verification, credential cleanup and the Shiny lifecycle. Live Oracle/client/provider compatibility remains unverified; there is no local Oracle identity demo.
